Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and the sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC accessed via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0), samples both sensors once per second, and appends each reading to a file named environmental_log.txt using the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]”, while handling any I2C or SPI communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions without crashing, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released and the program terminates gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, all without using any existing driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the digital output of a Keyes KY‑026 flame sensor module connected to the GPIO bus as a digital input on BCM pin 17, initializing the line for input with a pull‑down resistor, then polls the pin once every second, logging each reading to a CSV file named flame_events.log with columns timestamp, pin and state, and printing an alarm message to stdout whenever the sensor reports a HIGH (active HIGH on flame); the program must check the result of every driver library API call (the library’s API call*, the library’s API call*) and on any failure print an error message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, and it must clean up all GPIO resources both on normal termination and when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that monitors two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective proximity sensors connected via GPIO, with sensor 1 on GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 on GPIO17 (BCM), each providing a single active‑low open‑collector digital output with an internal pull‑up, and implements a debounce routine that reads each sensor five times spaced 2 ms apart and uses the majority value, logs the state once per second to the console as “0” for object present and “1” for no object, prints “ALERT: Both sensors detect object” when both sensors report object presence simultaneously, checks the return status of every API call and exits with a clear error message on failure, and installs a SIGINT handler that releases all GPIO resources on termination, while respecting the constraint that the B5W-DB01 has no analog output and that no driver, library, or deprecated code may be used.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads soil moisture from a YL‑69 soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC on SPI channel 0, CE0, operating at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor wired to MCP3008 channel 0; the program must sample every 60 seconds, convert the raw ADC value (expected between 300 and 800) to a moisture percentage using a calculate_moisture_level function, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage” to a file named soil_moisture_log.csv as well as print the same line to the console, while handling errors by checking driver library initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open, printing an error and retrying after a delay on SPI transfer failure without exiting, printing an error and continuing on file open failure, and ensuring proper cleanup on SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag in a signal_handler that closes the SPI handle, terminates the driver library, and exits cleanly, with all resources released on error paths such as terminating the driver library before returning if SPI open fails; the source must include the headers driver library.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, string.h, define the constants SPI_CHANNEL(0), SPI_BAUD(1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL(0), READ_DELAY(60), MIN_ADC(300), MAX_ADC(800), LOG_FILE("soil_moisture_log.csv"), and implement the functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output wired to GPIO17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, polling the pin every 50 ms and applying a 200 ms debounce delay after any state change followed by a re‑read to confirm motion, then upon confirmed motion triggers a camera snapshot saved as a JPEG with a filename containing the documented value and an ISO 8601 timestamp in the directory /home/pi/security_cam/; the program must initialize the driver, verify that initialization succeeded, construct the output path safely with snprintf, ensure the target directory exists before attempting capture, launch libcamera‑still using fork and execvp (never system()), check the child’s exit status and treat any non‑zero result as a capture error, log all key events—including startup, motion detection, capture success or failure, and shutdown—to syslog, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by stopping the main loop, releasing driver resources, and closing syslog.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the CSI bus device supplied as a command‑line argument (default /dev/video0), configures the camera for an 8‑bit grayscale format, sets up memory‑mapped streaming with a single buffer, and then continuously dequeues frames, handling the EAGAIN condition by using select() with a 2‑second timeout, saving each frame as a sequential .pgm file named image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, and so on; the program must include robust error handling for every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, must gracefully handle EAGAIN when dequeuing buffers, must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, and must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that stop streaming and safely unmap the buffers, while never using the C++ API of libcamera.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam attached as /dev/video0, uses memory‑mapped buffers to retrieve each frame, monitors the device asynchronously with select() to avoid indefinite blocking, and writes a line containing the timestamp of every captured frame in the form “seconds.microseconds” to a file named frame_log.txt; the implementation must include robust error handling for every driver ioctl, all file operations, and the memory‑mapping steps, must release all resources cleanly on every exit path, and must support a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT is received, while strictly adhering to the documented MJPEG format and avoiding any use of external video‑capture libraries.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that opens the CSI camera exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2 on the /dev/video0 bus, configures exactly four buffers sized according to the documented YUYV format, captures video frames, fragments each frame into UDP datagrams not exceeding 65 000 bytes, and prefixes each datagram with a header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragments, and payload size before sending the packets to a specified target IP and port; the program must invoke the required API calls on the command line as `./program <the library's API call> <the library's API call>`, rigorously check the result of every system call (open, ioctl, mmap, socket, sendto, etc.) and exit gracefully on error, run continuously until it receives SIGINT or SIGTERM, and then cleanly stop streaming, unmap all buffers and close every opened descriptor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0 in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK), queries the device capabilities to ensure both V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are present, sets the pixel format to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG with a width of 192 (the documented value) and V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests four MMAP buffers, starts streaming, dequeues a single frame, verifies that the dequeued buffer’s bytesused field is greater than zero, and writes the raw MJPEG bytes directly to a file named image.jpg without any re‑encoding; every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen call must have its return value checked and any failure reported with a descriptive perror/errno message, and a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to stop streaming, unmap all buffers, free the buffer array, close the file and the device file descriptor on all exit paths, ensuring clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor by polling its PWM‑style output on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), measuring the high‑pulse width and total cycle width with a busy‑wait loop using microsecond‑resolution timestamps obtained from the library’s call() API, sampling once every 5 seconds and applying a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file “temperature_log.txt” opens in append mode, compute the temperature while guarding against division by zero if the low‑time (TL) is zero, flag any reading outside the valid range of –40 °C to +150 °C as an error, and after three consecutive failures write a “SENSOR MALFUNCTION” entry to the log, logging each valid reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the file and releasing the driver library resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented high‑repeatability, clock‑stretching‑disabled measurement command, validates the 8‑bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words, and, after waiting at least 15 ms for the 6‑byte result, converts the raw values to degrees Celsius and percent relative humidity with the standard Sensirion formulas, then adds a sinusoidal offset of ±2 °C and ±5 % RH over a one‑hour period to simulate a greenhouse environment before logging each reading with an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp to a file named “environmental_data.txt” every 5 seconds; if any I2C read/write or CRC check fails, the program must retry up to three times with a one‑second delay and, after exhausting retries, log NaN values, while also providing robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C open/read/write, and file open, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the approximately 45 ms conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte block containing pressure, temperature and scale factor each followed by an 8‑bit CRC‑8 checksum (using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor), validates those CRCs, converts the raw data to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius with the sensor‑specified formulas, and logs a timestamp together with the pressure and temperature values to a CSV file named “airflow.csv” at a rate of one entry per second; the program must also detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented single‑shot high‑repeatability measurement command with clock‑stretching disabled, waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the command before reading the six‑byte result, sampling every five seconds, validating both CRC‑8 checksums with the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each reading to a CSV file named environment.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by temperature in Celsius and relative humidity in percent, inserting a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty; the program must check the driver initialization, opening of the I2C bus, every I2C read/write operation, CRC validation, and file opening, printing a descriptive error to stderr on any failure and either continuing or exiting as appropriate, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that performs a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the sensor library’s shutdown call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 temperature and humidity sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3) using the documented I2C address, polling each measurement until data is available or a 100 ms timeout expires, reading three bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each value and verifying the CRC‑8 checksum with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging a line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named environment.log with a header “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent” and ISO‑8601 timestamps, writing “ERROR” in place of the numeric fields together with a descriptive message to stderr whenever an I2C or CRC error occurs, checking the return value of every system call, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or NACK, and on any read failure issuing the documented sensor reset command before the next cycle; the program must also install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and exits gracefully, thereby simulating a greenhouse monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, initiates continuous measurement with the documented command, waits the required conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte response containing pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC and three scale‑factor bytes, validates the CRC‑8 for both pressure and temperature raw values, converts the raw data to floating‑point pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), and logs each sample once per second to a binary file named airflow.dat with pressure followed by temperature as floats while keeping the file handle open across samples; the program must check driver initialization, I2C opening, command write and read results, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, terminates the driver, and closes the file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads the differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus (bus 1) using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and then logging the results to stdout once every second; the implementation must open the I2C bus, verify successful driver initialization, perform a 9‑byte read that contains pressure, temperature and their respective scale factors, validate the CRC‑8 on each 3‑byte word using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle any CRC mismatch, sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions on every read/write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM close the I2C handle and invoke the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

    int i2c_bus;
    int i2c_addr;
} mlx90833_t;

int mlx90833_init(mlx90833_t *dev) {
    dev->i2c_bus = open(I2C_BUS, O_RDWR);
    if (dev->i2c_bus < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C bus");
        return -1;
    }

    if (ioctl(dev->i2c_bus, I2C_SLAVE, dev->i2c_addr) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(dev->i2c_bus);
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int mlx90833_read_register(mlx90833_t *dev, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    uint8_t buffer[1];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(dev->i2c_bus, buffer, 1) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to write to I2C register");
        return -1;
    }

    if (read(dev->i2c_bus, buffer, 1) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to read from I2C register");
        return -1;
    }

    *value = buffer[0];
    return 0;
}

int mlx90833_read_pressure(mlx90833_t *dev, int16_t *pressure) {
    uint8_t reg = MLX90833_REG_PRESSURE;
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    if (mlx90833_read_register(dev, reg, &buffer[0]) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    if (mlx90833_read_register(dev, reg + 1, &buffer[1]) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    *pressure = (int16_t)(buffer[0] << 8 | buffer[1]);
    return 0;
}

void signal_handler(int signum) {
    printf("\nCaught signal %d, exiting...\n", signum);
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main() {
    mlx90833_t dev;
    dev.i2c_bus = -1;
    dev.i2c_addr = MLX90833_ADDR;

    if (mlx90833_init(&dev) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize MLX90833 sensor\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    struct sigaction sa;
    sa.sa_handler = signal_handler;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;
    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to install SIGINT handler");
        close(dev.i2c_bus);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to install SIGTERM handler");
        close(dev.i2c_bus);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;

    int16_t pressure;
    time_t prev_time = time(NULL);
    while (1) {
        time_t current_time = time(NULL);
        if (current_time - prev_time >= 500) {
            prev_time = current_time;

            struct tm *tm_info = localtime(&current_time);
            char timestamp[20];
            strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm_info);
            printf("%s: Pressure = %d Pa\n", timestamp, pressure);
        }

        usleep(10000); // 10ms delay to avoid busy waiting
    }

        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(dev->i2c_bus);
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int mlx90833_read_register(mlx90833_t *dev, uint8_t reg, uint8_t *value) {
    uint8_t buffer[1];
    buffer[0] = reg;
    if (write(dev->i2c_bus, buffer, 1) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to write to I2C register");
        return -1;
    }

    if (read(dev->i2c_bus, buffer, 1) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to read from I2C register");
        return -1;
    }

    *value = buffer[0];
    return 0;
}

int mlx90833_read_pressure(mlx90833_t *dev, int16_t *pressure) {
    uint8_t reg = MLX90833_REG_PRESSURE;
    uint8_t buffer[2];
    if (mlx90833_read_register(dev, reg, &buffer[0]) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    if (mlx90833_read_register(dev, reg + 1, &buffer[1]) < 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    *pressure = (int16_t)(buffer[0] << 8 | buffer[1]);
    return 0;
}

void signal_handler(int signum) {
    printf("\nCaught signal %d, exiting...\n", signum);
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main() {
    mlx90833_t dev;
    dev.i2c_bus = -1;
    dev.i2c_addr = MLX90833_ADDR;

    if (mlx90833_init(&dev) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize MLX90833 sensor\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    struct sigaction sa;
    sa.sa_handler = signal_handler;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;
    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to install SIGINT handler");
        close(dev.i2c_bus);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to install SIGTERM handler");
        close(dev.i2c_bus);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    int16_t pressure;
    time_t prev_time = time(NULL);
    while (1) {
        time_t current_time = time(NULL);
        if (current_time - prev_time >= 500) {
            prev_time = current_time;

            if (mlx90833_read_pressure(&dev, &pressure) < 0) {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read pressure from MLX90833 sensor\n");
                continue;
            }

            struct tm *tm_info = localtime(&current_time);
            char timestamp[20];
            strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm_info);
            printf("%s: Pressure = %d Pa\n", timestamp, pressure);
        }

        usleep(10000); // 10ms delay to avoid busy waiting
    }

    close(dev.i2c_bus);
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

typedef struct {
    int fd;
    int sensor_address;
} mlx90819_t;

int mlx90819_init(mlx90819_t *sensor) {
    sensor->fd = open(I2C_BUS, O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK);
    if (sensor->fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C bus");
        return -1;
    }

    if (ioctl(sensor->fd, I2C_SLAVE, sensor->sensor_address) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(sensor->fd);
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int mlx90819_read_pressure(mlx90819_t *sensor, int *pressure) {
    unsigned char reg = MLX90819_REGISTER_PRESSURE;
    unsigned char buffer[2];
    int ret;

    if (write(sensor->fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        perror("Failed to write register address");
        return -1;
    }

    if (read(sensor->fd, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("Failed to read pressure data");
        return -1;
    }

    *pressure = (buffer[0] << 8) | buffer[1];
    return 0;
}

void handle_signal(int sig) {
    printf("\nCaught signal %d, exiting...\n", sig);
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main() {
    mlx90819_t sensor;
    int pressure;
    struct timeval tv;
    struct tm *tm_info;
    char timestamp[64];
    int ret;

    sensor.sensor_address = MLX90819_ADDR;

    if (mlx90819_init(&sensor) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize MLX90819 sensor\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, handle_signal);
    signal(SIGTERM, handle_signal);

    while (1) {
        gettimeofday(&tv, NULL);
        tm_info = localtime(&tv.tv_sec);
        strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm_info);

        ret = mlx90819_read_pressure(&sensor, &pressure);
        if (ret == 0) {
            printf("%s %d\n", timestamp, pressure);
        } else {
            fprintf(stderr, "I2C communication failure\n");
        }

        sleep(1);
    }

    close(sensor.fd);
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

typedef struct {
    int fd;
    int sensor_address;
} mlx90819_t;

int mlx90819_init(mlx90819_t *sensor) {
    sensor->fd = open(I2C_BUS, O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK);
    if (sensor->fd < 0) {
        perror("Failed to open I2C bus");
        return -1;
    }

    if (ioctl(sensor->fd, I2C_SLAVE, sensor->sensor_address) < 0) {
        perror("Failed to set I2C slave address");
        close(sensor->fd);
        return -1;
    }

    return 0;
}

int mlx90819_read_pressure(mlx90819_t *sensor, int *pressure) {
    unsigned char reg = MLX90819_REGISTER_PRESSURE;
    unsigned char buffer[2];
    int ret;

    if (write(sensor->fd, &reg, 1) != 1) {
        perror("Failed to write register address");
        return -1;
    }

    if (read(sensor->fd, buffer, 2) != 2) {
        perror("Failed to read pressure data");
        return -1;
    }

    *pressure = (buffer[0] << 8) | buffer[1];
    return 0;
}

void handle_signal(int sig) {
    printf("\nCaught signal %d, exiting...\n", sig);
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main() {
    mlx90819_t sensor;
    int pressure;
    struct timeval tv;
    struct tm *tm_info;
    char timestamp[64];
    int ret;

    sensor.sensor_address = MLX90819_ADDR;

    if (mlx90819_init(&sensor) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize MLX90819 sensor\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, handle_signal);
    signal(SIGTERM, handle_signal);

    while (1) {
        gettimeofday(&tv, NULL);
        tm_info = localtime(&tv.tv_sec);
        strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm_info);

        ret = mlx90819_read_pressure(&sensor, &pressure);
        if (ret == 0) {
            printf("%s %d\n", timestamp, pressure);
        } else {
            fprintf(stderr, "I2C communication failure\n");
        }

        sleep(1);
    }

    close(sensor.fd);
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from an STTS2004 temperature sensor on the I2C bus, logs the temperature to stdout once per second, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the LED is set high when the temperature exceeds 28 °C and low when it falls below 27 °C; the program must check the result of every I2C read and every GPIO operation, and on repeated I2C failures it must log the errno details and exit cleanly, while handling SIGINT and SIGTERM by releasing all driver library resources, closing the I2C file descriptor, turning the LED off, and then exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev for I2C access, libgpiod for GPIO/LED control

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after initiating a measurement before reading the result, retrieving exactly nine bytes consisting of two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC byte, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC byte, and three bytes of scale‑factor data, validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initialization value, logging the measured values with timestamps to a file named flow_data.txt, handling any I2C communication errors or the sensor‑absent condition gracefully, and ensuring that all resources are released on every exit path by installing a signal handler for SIGINT that performs the required cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor on the I2C bus using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1 default) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1 default), waiting at least 20 ms after issuing a no‑hold command and sampling every 60 seconds, logging each reading to a file named environment.log in CSV format with columns timestamp, temperature_c, humidity_pct while also printing the same line to stdout, handling errors by retrying each I2C transaction up to three times, validating sensor presence at startup by reading its electronic ID or firmware revision and exiting with a non‑zero status after logging a timestamped error to both the log file and stderr if the sensor is absent, flushing the log after every write, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, while using the “Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold” and “Measure Temperature, No Master Hold” commands or alternatively the “Read Temperature from Previous RH Measurement” command and performing raw byte transfers rather than register‑addressed reads.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 20 ms after each trigger to allow conversion, and appends a line to enviro_log.txt every 5 seconds in the format “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent”; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus with error checking, gracefully handle any I2C communication failures or a missing sensor by skipping the log entry on error, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle and terminate the driver, running in an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the temperature from a Sensirion STS40 I2C temperature sensor on the I2C bus, waiting 10 ms after each trigger for the conversion to complete and sampling the value every 5 seconds, logging each reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named temperature_log.txt; the program must open the I2C device with open(), set the slave address using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read exactly three bytes (two data bytes and one CRC8 byte), verify the CRC8 using the Sensirion‑specified polynomial, and on any error condition—including failures to open the device, ioctl, read, write, CRC mismatch, or open the log file—print a descriptive message to stderr and then continue looping; it must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, and run indefinitely in an infinite loop.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors air‑duct pressure in a simulated HVAC system using the Sensirion SDP810‑500Pa differential pressure sensor on the I2C bus, triggering a measurement, waiting at least 50 ms, then reading the 9‑byte result (2 bytes pressure, 1 byte CRC, 2 bytes temperature, 1 byte CRC, 3 bytes scale factor) once per second, validating every I2C read and write as well as each CRC‑8 using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor, logging each successful sample to a file named hvac_pressure_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C, and on any I2C or CRC error writing an error line with the timestamp and continuing, checking the return of every initialization call (the two required library API calls and fopen) and exiting with an error message if any fails, and handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and calling the library’s cleanup API function before terminating.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that drives a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C, buffers CO₂, temperature and humidity readings in a thread‑safe circular buffer of capacity 100, and periodically persists the data to a timestamped CSV file in /var/log/scd40_data/ (creating the directory if it does not exist) with a header row, while logging any errors with timestamps to /var/log/scd40_error.log; the main loop must wait at least one second after issuing the start‑periodic‑measurement command before the first read, then read the sensor every five seconds, validating the CRC‑8 of each value using the polynomial and initial value documented for the device and, on any CRC failure or I2C read/write error, log the error and skip that reading; a separate logging thread must write the buffered records to the CSV file every sixty seconds, and the program must handle SIGINT by using a volatile sig_atomic_t running flag to stop the main loop, send the documented stop‑periodic‑measurement command, join the logging thread, flush any remaining buffered data to a final CSV file, close the I2C handle and cleanly terminate the driver without any resource leaks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over the I2C bus, waiting at least 45 ms after each trigger for the measurement to complete and sampling once per second, reading the required nine bytes (two bytes of differential pressure followed by a CRC, two bytes of temperature followed by a CRC, and two bytes of scale factor followed by a CRC), validating each CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each successful sample to a file named sdp810_log.txt in CSV format with columns timestamp, pressure_Pa, temperature_C; the program must handle I2C open, write, and read errors as well as CRC failures by logging the error and continuing operation, and it must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt closes the I2C handle, terminates any driver resources, closes the log file, and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10110 pressure sensor on the I2C bus, initializing the driver library and opening the I2C bus with proper error checking, then in a loop triggered every 5 seconds waits 10 ms after each trigger before reading the sensor, appends each sample to a file named environmental_data.txt in append mode flushing after each write, prefixes each line with an ISO 8601 timestamp and also prints the reading to stdout, handling any I2C read/write errors by printing a message to stderr and skipping that sample, and installs a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, after which the program closes the I2C handle, closes the file, and calls the library’s cleanup API call().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C, retrieving exactly six bytes per read (two pressure bytes, two temperature bytes, and two CRC bytes) while checking every I2C syscall for errors, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and verifying the CRC on each sensor read; after each trigger a 20 ms delay must be observed, the sensor should be polled once per second, and the result used to drive a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) where the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions and switches to a 5 Hz pattern (100 ms on, 100 ms off) whenever the measured pressure falls below 95 000 Pa, with the GPIO line requested, set to output, and toggled accordingly; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that safely closes the I2C file descriptor and releases the GPIO line before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient and object temperature from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus, logs the timestamped readings to a file named temperature_log.txt every 2 seconds, and controls a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan turns on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and turns off when it falls below 28 °C; the program must validate driver library initialization, opening the I2C bus, and each I2C read/write operation, retrying any failed read up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts and skipping logging for invalid readings, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the Sensirion SHT40 sensor on I2C bus 1, issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 10 ms, then reading exactly six bytes, and streams the live temperature and humidity values to a local HTTP server on port 8080 using the library’s API call to serve an HTML page that displays the current temperature and humidity while clamping humidity to the range 0‑100 %; the implementation must include robust error handling for I2C communication such as sensor absence or bus errors with up to three retries per read, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals appropriately.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs a measurement every 5 seconds, and appends each result to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv with lines formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX”; the program must include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h to compile without warnings, check the success of all initialization and I/O calls, log any read failure to stderr while skipping that entry, and install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl+C is pressed the I2C handle is closed, the driver library is terminated, and the program exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple amplifier and a solid‑state relay, communicating with the MAX6675 over SPI0 (using either CE0 or CE1 as appropriate) and driving the solid‑state relay from GPIO17 (BCM numbering); the program must read the temperature from the thermocouple at a 1 Hz rate, update the SSR duty cycle based on the PID output (scaled 0.0 to 1.0) over a 1‑second period, log each temperature reading to a file named reflow_log.csv, load the target temperature profile from profile.txt where each line contains time_seconds,target_temp_celsius, apply robust error handling for all SPI communication and GPIO control including sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling termination signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled greenhouse heater using a DS18B20 temperature sensor and a 12 V heater driven through a relay and hardware PWM; the DS18B20 data line must be connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7) on the 1‑wire bus accessed via the w1‑gpio kernel module at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, the relay enable line to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), and the PWM duty control to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) using the hardware PWM channel, while the program must accept command‑line arguments specifying the desired temperature setpoint and the PID gains Kp, Ki, and Kd, read the sensor periodically, validate the CRC of each DS18B20 reading and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, compute the PID output, set the appropriate PWM duty cycle and relay state, and log every 5 seconds to a file named greenhouse.log a line containing the timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output and PWM duty cycle; all I/O operations must be checked for errors, and the program must install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that on any exit path cleanly release resources by turning off the relay, setting PWM to zero, closing any opened file descriptors or device handles, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads humidity from an AHT20 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented address, triggering a measurement, waiting 80 ms, then reading the 6‑byte result while verifying that the status byte reports calibrated and not busy, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms pause between attempts, and logging each humidity reading together with a timestamp to the console; the program must poll the sensor every 5 seconds, activate a dehumidifier relay connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the humidity exceeds 60 % and deactivate it when the humidity falls below 55 %, handle the case where the sensor is absent or all retries fail by printing an error message to stderr without terminating, and respond to SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA on GPIO2 pin 3, SCL on GPIO3 pin 5) using the documented default address when SDO is tied to GND and falling back to the documented alternative address, applies the Bosch 64‑bit compensation formulas, rewrites the ctrl_meas register in forced mode each loop to trigger a new measurement, and appends a line to weather_data.txt every five seconds in the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa”, while checking every I/O call (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs) for errors, logging any sensor I/O failures to stderr and attempting to continue or exit gracefully, ensuring the sensor is powered from the 3.3 V rail only, and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to break the logging loop, close the I2C file descriptor and any open files, and exit with status 0.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reading and validating the 11‑word calibration table from the documented register before any sampling, and then, via a hardware timer callback that fires every 500 ms, obtains temperature and pressure using the BMP180 formulas with OSS = 0 (ensuring the temperature routine is not called from inside the pressure routine), stores each timestamped reading in a 60‑entry circular buffer, prints each new reading to stdout, and drives a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (active‑high) whenever the temperature exceeds 30 °C; the timer callback must remain simple and avoid blocking calls, every library API call’s return code must be checked and the sample skipped on error, and the program must handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces to a BMP180 sensor on the I2C bus using the documented address, reads the sensor’s calibration data and applies the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure in pascals, and toggles data logging on and off via a falling‑edge interrupt on GPIO27 with a 200 ms debounce; while logging is enabled the program must record a timestamp and the computed pressure to a file named pressure_log.txt every 2 seconds, must detect and recover from I2C communication errors and driver initialization failures, and must clean up all allocated resources and gracefully terminate when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier on SPI0 using CE0 (GPIO8 as chip‑select, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz, drives a solid‑state relay connected to GPIO17 with a PWM signal to modulate a resistive heater so that a PI controller with anti‑windup maintains a target temperature (default 25.0 °C) while never exceeding a safe maximum duty cycle of 80 %, logs each measurement and the applied duty cycle together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named heater_log.csv, and implements error handling such that any SPI read failure or any MAX31855 fault condition (open circuit, short to ground or VCC) causes the duty cycle to be set immediately to 0 % and the error to be recorded in the log while the program continues running, and also catches SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off the heater, closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, and terminates the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls the CPU temperature every 0.5 seconds and drives a common‑anode RGB LED attached to the GPIO bus with the Red cathode on GPIO17, Green cathode on GPIO18 and Blue cathode on GPIO27, using hardware PWM via the library’s API call() with a 0‑255 range and inverted duty (255 turns the channel off) while respecting the 3.3 V common‑anode supply and individual current‑limiting resistors; the program must open the temperature file, check the return value of the API call() each time it sets a PWM value and on any failure print an error message and exit with a non‑zero status, also handling fopen failure and short or failed reads by checking ferror, printing a diagnostic and skipping that update cycle, and on each loop iteration print to stdout the temperature in millidegrees Celsius together with the three PWM values; the LED color should be solid Blue (0,0,255) for temperatures below 40000 m°C, solid Green (0,255,0) for 40000‑59999 m°C, and solid Red (255,0,0) for 60000 m°C and above; a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, turn off all channels by writing a duty of 255, call the library’s API call() for cleanup, and allow the main loop to exit gracefully without calling exit() inside the handler, ensuring the file handle is closed on every code path and the program runs an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus with its data line on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), using the required start signal of pulling the line low for at least 1 ms, then captures the full 40‑bit response, validates the 8‑bit checksum, and posts the measured values as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity via HTTP; the implementation must gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent, checksum mismatches, and network errors by retrying up to three times, and must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a BMP180 sensor, configuring the sensor for oversampling setting OSS=3 and applying the full Bosch BMP180 integer‑only compensation algorithm, and that toggles data logging on and off with a push‑button connected to GPIO 4 configured for falling‑edge interrupts with the internal pull‑up; the interrupt handler must debounce using a driver‑library tick comparison of at least 200 000 µs, and when logging is enabled the program shall read pressure every 2 seconds, waiting the required 26 ms conversion delay, and append a timestamped pressure value in hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt, while printing a status message when logging is disabled; the code must check every I2C read/write return value, report any errors to stderr, fail cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid calibration data, and on receipt of SIGINT must close the I2C handle and release all driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected on the 1‑wire bus using GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) by issuing the start signal (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20‑40 µs, then release), captures the 40‑bit response with microsecond‑level edge timing, validates the checksum and, if the sensor is absent or the checksum fails, retries up to three times with a 2‑second backoff before giving up; the main loop must perform a read every 10 seconds, and each successful reading must be formatted as JSON and POSTed with Content‑Type: application/json to http://your‑the‑library’s‑API‑call.com/api/humidity, retrying the POST up to three times on network or HTTP errors and treating any non‑2xx response as a failure; the program must initialize the driver library with the library’s API call() and check for errors, log all events to syslog, accept a command‑line option “-s <url>” to override the default URL, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that calls the library’s API call() and curl_global_cleanup() on every exit path.

Write a C program for the Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler by reading the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and the current fan state from /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state, polling the temperature every 5 seconds, applying a tiered speed map where temperatures below 45 °C set the fan state to 0 (off), below 55 °C set state 1, below 65 °C set state 2, and 65 °C or higher set state 3 (maximum), first validating the cooling device’s max_state before any write, and writing the new state back to the same cooling_device sysfs entry only when the speed changes; each fan speed change must be logged with a timestamp to /var/log/fan_control.log, all file opens, reads, writes, and parses must be checked for errors with transient read failures simply causing the program to retry on the next cycle, and the program must handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by setting the fan to state 0, logging the shutdown event, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that implements a PID controller to maintain a target temperature of 50 °C by PWM‑controlling a resistive heater on GPIO18 using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑100 %; the program must read the current temperature from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CLK = GPIO11, CS = GPIO8/CE0, DO = GPIO9) at 500 kHz, acquiring 4 bytes per sample, and log every second to a file named heater_log.txt the measured temperature, the PWM duty cycle, and the PID output; the PID defaults are Kp = 1.0, Ki = 0.1, Kd = 0.01, and the controller must include error handling that parses the MAX31855 fault bits to detect open‑circuit, short‑to‑GND, or short‑to‑VCC conditions, logs any such errors, disables the heater and resets the PID state, and also enforces a failsafe that disables the heater if the reading exceeds 100 °C or falls below 0 °C; finally, the program must cleanly release resources on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the heater off, closing the SPI interface, and terminating any driver activity.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus to drive the PWM input of a Noctua NF‑A4x10 5V PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12), polling the CPU temperature every 5 seconds and mapping the temperature linearly to a 25 kHz PWM duty cycle where temperatures of 40 °C and below correspond to 0 % duty, 70 °C and above correspond to 100 % duty, and values in between are interpolated accordingly; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly, confirm that each PWM frequency and duty cycle call succeeds, and log each reading to a file named cooling_log.csv with a header and rows containing the timestamp, temperature in °C, and the PWM duty cycle percentage, while also handling any file I/O errors, and it must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning the fan off and releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1, assuming the sensors are attached through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout or a comparable I2C hub, and polls each sensor once per second, reading three bytes from each (two data bytes followed by a CRC‑8 byte) while validating the checksum and retrying up to three times on any I2C error before giving up on that read; when a valid reading is obtained, the program must append a line to flow_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2”, skipping the entry if the CRC check fails, and it must handle a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing all I2C handles and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall‑Effect latch sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with Channel A wired to GPIO17 and Channel B to GPIO18, configuring the pins as open‑drain outputs with internal pull‑up resistors enabled, implementing a 2‑bit quadrature state machine that resolves 360 pulses per revolution into a normalized angular position ranging from 0.00 to 360.00 degrees, logging each timestamped position change to a file named encoder_log.txt, providing robust error handling for both GPIO initialization and file I/O operations, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal by using the driver library’s cleanup facilities.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, and logs each measurement to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt with columns timestamp, red, and ir; the program must also monitor the infrared reading and activate an LED connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the IR value exceeds a threshold of 2000, while robustly handling I2C read/write errors and conditions where the sensor is absent, and it must cleanly release all resources—including the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and the log file—on any exit path by catching SIGINT and SIGTERM signals for graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor by counting its pulses on the GPIO bus, using GPIO18 (physical pin 12) configured as an input with a pull‑down resistor, counting only rising edges and assuming one pulse per revolution; the program must calculate the RPM over a 1‑second interval, protect the pulse counter with a pthread mutex shared between the interrupt service routine and the main thread, log each RPM value together with a timestamp to rpm_log.txt in append mode flushing the file immediately, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by terminating the driver library, closing the log file, and destroying the mutex, while also handling the case of a missing sensor by logging 0.00 RPM when no pulses are detected.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that communicates over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor using the documented address, samples the sensor every 100 ms, logs each timestamped reading to a CSV file named adpd144ri_log.txt, and triggers an LED connected to GPIO17 whenever the infrared reading exceeds a threshold of 2000; the implementation must robustly handle I2C errors and the case where the sensor is absent, and must clean up all resources—including the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and the log file—on every exit path, also handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, while avoiding any use of deprecated driver libraries or driver library components.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that samples the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier connected via GPIO, using the OUT pin (audio signal) on GPIO17 as an input and the GAIN select pin on GPIO18 as an output (set GPIO18 LOW to select 60 dB gain), polls the digital input every 10 ms to rapidly detect rising edges that indicate peak sound events, logs each detected event to a file named audio_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL” where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge, prints a startup message, and runs indefinitely until interrupted, while handling all driver library initialization and I/O errors robustly by checking the return value of every API call and ensuring clean release of all driver library resources on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the flow rate of a microfluidic drug delivery system using a Sensirion SLF3S‑4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected to I2C bus 1, reading the sensor every 1000 ms by retrieving three bytes (a two‑byte MSB‑first raw value followed by a CRC‑8 byte that must be validated with the documented polynomial and initial value), logging each successful measurement to a CSV file named flow_log.csv in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min” with the file opened once at startup in append mode, kept open, and flushed after each write; the program must check driver initialization, I2C open, write, and read operations, log any I2C read/write failures to stderr and attempt recovery on the next loop iteration, log a CRC failure as an error and skip that reading, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Honeywell MICS‑VZ‑89TE VOC sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the sensor data, computes an indoor air quality (IAQ) index, and logs a timestamped line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named air_quality_log.csv containing the IAQ value together with TVOC in ppb and eCO₂ in ppm; the implementation must check every I2C read and write return value, detect and handle conditions where the sensor is absent or the bus reports an error without crashing, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt gracefully closes the I2C interface, flushes and closes the log file, and terminates the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line wired to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering, physical pin 11) as an input with the consumer label “ttp223_tamper”, polling the line every 100 ms based on CLOCK_MONOTONIC; the program must detect when the TTP223B output, which is HIGH while touched and LOW when released, remains continuously HIGH for more than 5 seconds, then print a single intrusion alert to stdout for that touch event and reset the timer when the sensor is released so that alerts are not repeated for the same touch, while checking every library call for failure and printing strerror(errno) on error, and if a sensor read fails mid‑loop printing an error and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE after performing cleanup; the cleanup routine must also be invoked on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM to gracefully release the line and close the chip on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that runs as a daemon and continuously polls the SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to the GPIO bus on pin GPIO23 (BCM numbering), using a pull‑down resistor on the input to keep the line low when dry, reading the sensor every 2 seconds and generating an alert whenever a logic HIGH is detected; on each detection the program must print an alert message to stdout and append a line to a file named flood_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected”, while also checking that the driver library initializes correctly and, if a GPIO read fails, logging an error entry to the same file and scheduling an automatic re‑initialization attempt after 60 seconds; the daemon must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to release all resources cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM 23) and to drive an LED on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18) with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor, polling the sensor every 50 ms so that the LED is illuminated only while the sensor is actively touched; the program must open the GPIO chip, request the input line for the sensor and the output line for the LED, check the return status of every driver call including chip opening, line requests, reads and writes, handle the situation where the GPIO chip is unavailable, log startup, shutdown, each touch event and any errors to the system syslog using openlog/syslog, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to capture rising‑edge events and toggles an LED attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) on each detected touch; the program must employ the line event interface to wait for rising edges rather than polling, apply a software debounce of approximately 50 ms after each rising‑edge detection, initialize the LED line as an output and drive it LOW at startup, verify the result of every driver call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print clear error messages to stderr when a call fails, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by gracefully releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously polls two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors on the GPIO bus—sensor 1 connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO17 (BCM)—with a 50 ms loop to debounce, drives LED 1 on GPIO27 (BCM) and LED 2 on GPIO22 (BCM) such that each LED is lit while its corresponding sensor is touched (sensors are active‑high digital outputs), records every touch and release event in a 100‑entry in‑RAM circular buffer storing the sensor pin number, a Unix timestamp, and the new state while maintaining an overflow counter, checks the return value of every API call and prints a diagnostic to stderr on any failure, handles SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that turns off both LEDs, calls the required API cleanup function, and on shutdown prints the full contents of the log buffer together with the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Raindrop Sensor Module with a digital output connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, enabling the internal pull‑up resistor on that pin so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected, and polls the pin every 500 ms; the program must detect the active‑low condition where a LOW (0) level indicates rain and a HIGH (1) level indicates no rain, and it should write timestamped “Rain Detected” or “No Rain” messages to /var/log/rain_events.log only when the state changes, while checking the return value of every driver library call and of fopen, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the log file and releases any driver resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors a rotating shaft’s RPM by reading two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall‑Effect sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO18 (BCM), applying approximately a 5 ms debounce to each state change, logging every transition to a CSV file named shaft_log.txt in the format “timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state”, printing the calculated RPM to the console, handling any GPIO initialization failures or file I/O errors gracefully, including the standard headers such as errno.h and string.h to ensure clean compilation, and guaranteeing that all resources are released properly on every exit path, including handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform orderly cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C optical sensor on I2C bus 1, pausing one second between each read, and appends each measurement to a file named biometric_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%” while flushing the file after every write; the program must use the driver library for I2C access, check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, print any communication errors to stderr and keep running, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl‑C is pressed it gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors the structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors (Omron D7E-3) connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 on GPIO17 (BCM) and sensor 2 on GPIO18 (BCM), both configured as inputs with internal pull‑down resistors enabled, and drives an alarm (buzzer/LED) on GPIO27 (BCM) which is active‑high and initialized LOW; the program must poll each sensor every 100 ms via the library’s API call, log ISO‑8601 timestamps (YYYY‑MM‑DDTHH:MM:SS) to a file named bridge_integrity.log for tilt‑start, threshold‑exceeded, and tilt‑end events, activate the alarm if either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, deactivate the alarm when both sensors return to LOW, include error handling that checks the driver library initialization, the log file opening, and the API call return values, and implement clean shutdown handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates the alarm, closes the log file, calls the library’s API cleanup, and guarantees the alarm is off on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Omron D7S‑A0011 seismic sensor on I2C bus 1 using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM), polls the sensor every 100 ms, detects earthquake‑like events when the Euclidean vibration magnitude exceeds a threshold of 500, logs each threshold‑exceeding event to a file named seismic_events.log with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value, turns on an alert LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) for 1 second for each such event, initializes the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power‑down bit in CTRL1, handles I2C communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions with up to three retries per read, and on receipt of Ctrl+C/SIGINT cleanly releases the I2C handle, the driver library, and closes the log file; the program must be built with gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lthe driver library -lm -lrt.
